Lessons.Title: Round Doubloons
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: understand rounding decimals to the nearest whole number, tenth and hundredth as choosing the closest mark on an appropriately labeled number line. The source starts with a scale whose displayed reading is less precise than the objects on the pan; the displayed reading must not be treated as an exact measurement.

Warm-up — digital scales: a modeled balance has weights whose exact mass totals 12.32 ounces, while a tenths-precision scale displays 12.3. Give different possible reasons and explain that 12.3 ounces need not equal exactly 12.300; a measurement device may report the nearest tenth instead of every hundredth.

Activity 1 — historical coin comparison without copyrighted art: the publisher's public page gives two historical sample weights, 6.867 and 6.766 grams. On a number line to hundredths, the first is closest to 6.87 and the second to 6.77; to tenths the values round to 6.9 and 6.8. Both round to 7 grams at whole-gram precision, so that coarser scale cannot distinguish their weights. Use two independent textual positions instead of reproducing coin photographs.

Activity 2 — choose precision: write original values 5.743 and 5.748 grams and locate each between adjacent hundredths. To the nearest hundredth, 5.743 becomes 5.74 and 5.748 becomes 5.75, while to the nearest tenth both display 5.7. Explain what distinguishable information is lost at lower precision.

Assessment: the original source asks learners to reason about historical coin identification and how scale precision changes claims; teacher reviews number-line placement, device interpretation and why rounded equal values do not establish equal original masses. One rounded number is only a numeric subcheck.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rounding as closest benchmark
KeyConcepts.Definition: A number rounded to a named place is represented by the closest multiple of that place unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 6.867 is nearer 6.87 than 6.86 and becomes 6.87 to hundredths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Use a labeled number line to compare distances.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coarse display can hide differences
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distinct exact masses may produce the same display when the scale records only coarse units.
KeyConcepts.Example: Equal rounded results need not imply equal original measurements.

KeyConcepts.Title: Precision matters to interpretation
KeyConcepts.Definition: The same exact value can round differently to different place values.
KeyConcepts.Example: Named unit and rounding place must be explicit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Historical sample coin masses
WorkedExamples.Question: Round 6.867 grams and 6.766 grams to nearest tenth, hundredth and whole.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: Locate 6.867 between 6.86 and 6.87; locate 6.766 between 6.76 and6.77.
Round to hundredths: 6.87 and6.77; to tenths:6.9 and6.8.
To whole grams choose 7 for both.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Hundredths: 6.87 and 6.77; tenths: 6.9 and 6.8; whole: both 7 grams.

WorkedExamples.Title: Concealed hundredths on a scale
WorkedExamples.Question: A scale reports12.3 ounces though exact measured pieces total12.32. Is its display necessarily wrong?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: State that the scale may only report tenths.
Round 12.32 to the nearest tenth.
Compare the displayed 12.3 with the rounded value.
WorkedExamples.Check: The displayed precision is not sufficient to recover the exact hundredths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a precision that distinguishes masses
WorkedExamples.Question: Rounded to hundredths and tenths, compare5.743 and5.748 grams.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: At hundredths, 5.743 is near5.74, 5.748 is near5.75.
At tenths, both are near5.7.
Explain which display can distinguish them.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Hundredths distinguish 5.74 and5.75; tenths produce the same 5.7.
WorkedExamples.Check: The exact masses are still different.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume identical rounded measurements prove equal exact values
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Rounding loses information about less-significant places.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State possible underlying intervals rather than identifying an exact original mass.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Rounding to tenths and hundredths may give different displays.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the unit interval on a number line before selecting a closest value.

SummaryPoints: Rounding chooses the closest value at the requested place, not an exact hidden measurement.
Coarse measurement can make distinct masses appear identical.
The source's measured-coin interpretation and number-line explanation remain teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Round Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: label number-line endpoints and tick intervals correctly, estimate a point, and round decimals to the nearest whole number, tenth or hundredth with a defensible place-value explanation. The source first asks children to critique an incorrectly located 15.53 and then continues with more number lines.

Warm-up — poorly labeled point: an original unmarked 0–1 line has a marker slightly left of its midpoint. Give a too-low, reasonable and too-high decimal estimate; a picture without tenths marks cannot justify one exact thousandth. Propose adding tenths to improve the estimate.

Activity 1 — check a location: in a number line from 15.5 to15.6, a point representing 15.53 should be 3/10 of the distance across the interval from15.5 and closer to15.5 than15.6. A placement more than halfway toward15.6 is incorrect even if its numeric label is 15.53. Draw and label all tenths and hundredths before reasoning.

Activity 2 — round from nested lines: the original first-party decimal 6.273 lies between 6 and7, between6.2 and6.3, and between6.27 and6.28. Its nearest whole is6, nearest tenth6.3 and nearest hundredth6.27. Another example 4.685 lies between4.68 and4.69 and at the hundredth midpoint; under conventional half-up rounding it becomes4.69, but any alternate tie convention must be specified before grading.

Assessment: source asks students to label previously blank tick marks and explain if a plotted point is accurate before rounding. Numeric rounding answers do not establish correct number-line construction or critique. Student-generated diagrams and justification are teacher-reviewed.

KeyConcepts.Title: A number line's labels define location
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal tick spacing must correspond to equal numeric increments.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 15.53 is 0.03 beyond15.5, or 30% of a 0.1-wide interval.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rounding by closest value
KeyConcepts.Definition: To round to tenths or hundredths, compare the number with adjacent multiples of the target place value.
KeyConcepts.Example: A number line or place-value chart explains the choice.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tie conventions should be stated
KeyConcepts.Definition: Exactly halfway between two rounded choices can require an explicit rule.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Under conventional half-up, 4.685 rounds to 4.69 to hundredths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Do not treat unannounced alternative tie-breaking as a source-mandated fact.

WorkedExamples.Title: Critique an incorrectly plotted point
WorkedExamples.Question: A pupil marks15.53 closer to15.6 than to15.5. Is that accurate?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: Compare the interval width of0.1 and see that the point is30% of the way from15.5.
Explain why it belongs closer to15.5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Distance to15.5 is0.03; distance to15.6 is0.07.

WorkedExamples.Title: Round 6.273 to three places
WorkedExamples.Question: Round6.273 to nearest whole, tenth and hundredth.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: Locate6.273 between6 and7; nearer6.
Locate6.273 between6.2 and6.3; nearer6.3.
Locate6.273 between6.27 and6.28; nearer6.27.
WorkedExamples.Check: Rounding must follow the requested place, not the number of printed digits.

WorkedExamples.Title: A midpoint requires a rule
WorkedExamples.Question: How does 4.685 round to hundredths under nearest, halves-up?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: The hundredth choices are4.68 and4.69.
4.685 is exactly halfway between them.
Apply the specified halves-up convention.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not infer a tie policy from an unlabeled source or use floating-point approximations as evidence.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume a decimal label is correctly located because its digits match
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A point must correspond to the actual fraction of the scaled interval.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the point's relative distance to labeled endpoints.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use the thousandths digit to round directly to the whole place
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Rounding to a place depends first on the next smaller place.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose the requested place, then determine nearest available benchmark.

SummaryPoints: Label and interpret number-line scales before placing or rounding decimals.
Different rounding precisions may give different displays of the same exact number.
Source point placement and mathematical explanation require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Order Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare, order and generate numbers lying STRICTLY between two decimals using place value, optionally supported by number lines. The source intentionally explores the possibility of a number between two consecutive thousandths, even if students cannot yet NAME that number using only three decimal places.

Warm-up — true or false: 0.909>0.91 is false because0.909<0.910; 4.1<4.100 is false since they are equal; 0.99<0.999 is true. Require a verbal place-value explanation rather than comparing written digit counts.

Activity 1 — choose multiple valid values between endpoints: 786.2<786.254<786.3, 9.99<9.995<10, 0.45<0.456<0.46, 0.5<0.507<0.51, and0.99<0.995<0.999. Draw a number line with suitable endpoints for one chosen inequality and compare different students' answers; there is no single value each blank must contain.

Activity 2 — the midpoint question: ask whether any number lies between 1.731 and1.732. There is no thousandth-grid value between consecutive thousandths, BUT at finer precision 1.7315 is strictly between. Invite students to conjecture and explain what a more finely subdivided number line would reveal, without requiring formal fourth-decimal-place notation from every Grade 5 learner.

Activity 3 — order an original set 0.907,0.97,0.917 and0.9. Express them as 0.907,0.970,0.917 and0.900 to compare, yielding 0.900<0.907<0.917<0.970. A teacher reviews the argument and choice of scale and should not mark the absence of more advanced naming as automatically wrong.

Assessment: numerical ordering can be checked exactly, but the student-generated intervals, exploratory finer-precision conjecture, ordering diagrams and peer revisions are teacher-reviewed. Gated source response and figure cards are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Strict decimal intervals
KeyConcepts.Definition: A number in an open interval must be greater than the lower endpoint and less than the upper endpoint.
KeyConcepts.Example: Multiple choices can satisfy one problem.

KeyConcepts.Title: Trailing zeros preserve order
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equivalent decimal notation can make comparisons easier.
KeyConcepts.Example: More printed digits do not imply a greater number.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decimals beyond thousandths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Even when two displayed decimals are consecutive thousandths, a finer decimal representation can lie strictly between.
KeyConcepts.Example: The source invites conceptual observation without imposing an unintroduced algorithm.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fill a strict inequality
WorkedExamples.Question: Give a decimal strictly between9.99 and10.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: Express endpoints as9.990 and10.000.
Choose9.995, five thousandths above the lower endpoint.
Verify it is below10.000.

WorkedExamples.Title: More precise numbers between
WorkedExamples.Question: Is there a number between1.731 and1.732?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: Observe they are consecutive thousandth-place numbers.
Consider splitting the gap into two equal smaller parts.
Locate the midpoint using a fourth decimal place if familiar.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, for example1.7315; a finer representation is needed.
WorkedExamples.Check: 1.731<1.7315<1.732; teacher checks the learner's reasoning at their introduced precision.

WorkedExamples.Title: Order four decimals
WorkedExamples.Question: Put0.907,0.97,0.917,0.9 from least to greatest.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: Rewrite each with three places:0.907,0.970,0.917,0.900.
Compare tenths first, then hundredths and thousandths.
Order from smallest to largest.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Conclude no real value lies between consecutive thousandths
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A new fractional place can subdivide the interval again.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explore a finer number line without demanding unsupported curriculum mastery.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat 0.9 as greater than 0.907 because it has fewer digits
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Trailing zeros have no effect on decimal magnitude.

SummaryPoints: An open decimal interval may have many valid choices and requires strict inequalities.
Ordering should use place value and equivalent trailing zeros.
Finer-number-line conjectures and student-authored values require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Solve Problems with Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use rounding precision to determine how closely recorded decimal measurements can distinguish athletes' finishing times and speed, and reason about sets of possible underlying thousandth-place values. The source's luge data are CREATED for instruction, not actual event results.

Warm-up: an original, entirely hypothetical four-athlete sled-race table records times in seconds 52.146,52.153,52.178,52.201. Ask what the unlabeled columns might mean before naming units, and discuss why a race result uses smaller elapsed time even if maximum speed rewards larger measures.

Activity 1 — compare rounding precisions: to nearest second all four record52; to nearest tenth the first three record52.1, the fourth52.2; to nearest hundredth the first records52.15 and the second52.15, creating a tie absent from the original thousandth times. To thousandths the fastest is52.146, then52.153,52.178 and52.201. Explain why rounding can erase distinctions without changing the actual times.

Activity 2 — reverse rounding: assuming a recorded time is itself specified to thousandth-second precision and ties are rounded half-up, which thousandth times display52.15 when rounded to nearest hundredth? The ten discrete values52.145,52.146,...,52.154 do. Alternatively a measurement of52.615 to nearest thousandth rounds to52.62 at hundredths. State precision and midpoint convention; the result for underlying continuous times is an interval, not just ten measurements.

Assessment: the source asks learners to create mathematical questions from an unlabeled race table, discuss how rankings change under various recording precisions and explain possible pre-rounded values. Teacher review is required for the contextual explanation and inverse-rounding interval; a single rounded numeric value is a subcheck. Neither source luge photo nor any actual athletic record is asserted or reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rounding can create apparent ties
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distinct exact values may round to the same display at lower precision.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 52.146 and52.153 both become52.15 when rounded to hundredths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Rounding is not a tie in actual time.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measurement resolution changes rankings
KeyConcepts.Definition: Competition ranking is based on original elapsed times; coarser recording may remove ordering information.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse rounding describes a set
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rounded hundredth value can arise from multiple finer values, depending on the stated midpoint convention.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 52.145 through52.154 in thousandths round to52.15 by half-up.
KeyConcepts.Example: Continuous underlying values lie in an interval around the rounded hundredth.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare race rankings at different precisions
WorkedExamples.Question: Four athletes have times52.146,52.153,52.178,52.201 seconds. How do their reported results change?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: Order the original thousandth times, with smaller faster.
Round to hundredths:52.15,52.15,52.18,52.20.
Round to tenths:52.1,52.2,52.2,52.2; round to whole seconds:52,52,52,52.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Exact fastest:52.146. Hundredths tie first two; tenths tie last three; whole seconds tie all.
WorkedExamples.Check: Tie claims are about rounded displays, not original elapsed times.

WorkedExamples.Title: Which thousandths round to one hundredth?
WorkedExamples.Question: Which thousandth-second displays round to52.15 seconds to nearest hundredth, half-up?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: The lower midpoint is52.145 and the upper is52.155.
Include values from52.145 but exclude52.155 which rounds to52.16.
List allowed thousandth increments.

WorkedExamples.Title: Change the recorded precision
WorkedExamples.Question: Round52.615 seconds from thousandths to nearest hundredth under half-up.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value reasoning, accessible number-line description and exact decimal arithmetic.
Steps: The nearest hundredth candidates are52.61 and52.62.
52.615 is exactly halfway.
Apply the stated halves-up rule.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not silently replace the named tie rule with a different algorithm.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim a rounded tie proves equal actual athlete times
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different finer values can map to one rounded display.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the exact source times and label any tie as display-level only.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Infer a unique thousandth from one hundredth rounded value
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Rounding to hundredths removes information about multiple finer values.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the interval and rounding rule before enumerating possible original measurements.

SummaryPoints: Rounding a race time can create apparent ties and change displayed rank groups.
Inverse rounding to a stated resolution gives a range of finer measurements.
The original source's table questions, explanations and interpretation require teacher review.
